title: Final checks: SAP S/4HANA migration testing and Amazon Relay logistics
seriesDescription: SAP S/4HANA migration, Amazon Relay and trip tracking, network digital twins, cloud-platform themes. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Company-domain concepts: S/4HANA data migration, reconciliation and test automation with a business knowledge graph, plus middle-mile logistics, tendering, load boards, ETA and event-driven trip tracking.
source: SAP Help Portal and SAP Community (S/4HANA Migration Cockpit: direct transfer, staging tables, simulation; Business Partner approach); Amazon Relay site and blog (load board, Post A Truck); FMCSA hours-of-service summary and visor card; Kafka documentation; general ERP migration practice

questions.prompt: Match each S/4HANA transition term to its meaning.

right.text: New implementation: you set up a fresh system and migrate chosen data
Convert the existing ECC system in place, keeping its configuration and data
Hybrid approach that moves selected data or company codes into a new or converted system
SAP tool that loads data through predefined migration objects
Intermediate tables where source data is placed and checked before it is loaded
Real-time replication of every database transaction

questions.explanation: Interviewers expect you to link the approach to testing scope: greenfield needs heavy data migration validation, brownfield needs heavy regression testing.

questions.prompt: A migration run reads 1,250,000 source rows. 3,500 are rejected by validation and 1,246,000 are loaded into S/4HANA. How many rows are unaccounted for?
questions.explanation: 1,250,000 - 3,500 - 1,246,000 = 500. Every source row must end up loaded, rejected (with a reason) or deliberately excluded; any remainder is a defect to investigate.

questions.prompt: A legacy system has 10,000 customers and 2,000 vendors, of which 500 are the same organisation (both customer and vendor). In S/4HANA, customers and vendors are created as `Business Partners;` one partner can hold both roles. How many Business Partners should you expect if the 500 are merged into one each?
questions.explanation: 10,000 + 2,000 - 500 = 11,500. In S/4HANA the Business Partner is the leading object for customer and vendor master data, so duplicates should be matched and merged during migration.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: In S/4HANA, customer and vendor master data are maintained through the Business Partner.
questions.reason: One Business Partner can hold several roles, such as customer and supplier, which avoids duplicate master records.

whys.a: Correct: the Business Partner is the single central record and roles describe how it is used.
whys.b: R is the mechanism behind A.

questions.explanation: Expect questions on customer/vendor integration (CVI) and how legacy duplicates are matched before migration.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: The migration cockpit can simulate a migration to validate data before it is actually posted.
questions.reason: Migration objects can be filled from templates or from staging tables.

whys.a: R is true but concerns data input, not simulation.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true but independent; simulation checks the data against the target rules without creating records.

questions.explanation: Run simulation repeatedly to burn down data-quality errors before the real load.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: If the source and target row counts are equal, the migration is correct.
questions.reason: Counts can match even when values were mapped incorrectly or records were swapped.

whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: A is false, R is true. Reconcile also control totals (amounts, balances) and sampled or hashed field values.

questions.explanation: A layered check: counts, then totals per key (for example per company code), then field-level comparison on samples or full hashes.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Mock cutover runs rehearse timing and uncover data-quality issues before go-live.
questions.reason: A mock cutover permanently replaces the production system.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: A is true; R is false because a mock cutover runs in a non-production system, with the real cutover reserved for go-live.

questions.explanation: Measure each mock run: duration per object, rejected rows, and reconciliation differences. Trends show readiness.

questions.prompt: Tables legacy_gl(company_code, amount) and s4_gl(company_code, amount) hold the general ledger amounts before and after migration. Write one SQL query that returns each company_code whose total amount differs between the two tables, including codes that exist in only one table.
questions.model:
SELECT company_code, SUM(amount) AS diff
FROM (SELECT company_code, amount FROM legacy_gl
      UNION ALL
      SELECT company_code, -amount FROM s4_gl) t
GROUP BY company_code
HAVING SUM(amount) <> 0;
questions.explanation: Other solutions pass: a FULL OUTER JOIN of two grouped subqueries with COALESCE, or EXCEPT in both directions. The UNION ALL with negated amounts handles codes that exist on one side only. Floating-point amounts should be compared with a tolerance or use DECIMAL.

questions.prompt: Why model business objects (customer, material, plant, open order) as a knowledge graph in a migration test programme?

options.text: Relationships are queryable, so you can trace which open orders break if a material fails to migrate.
options.why: Right: lineage and impact analysis follow edges instead of ad hoc joins.

options.text: A graph replaces the need for reconciliation because the relationships themselves prove that the data is right.
options.why: Relationships help trace issues but do not replace counts, totals and value checks.

options.text: Graphs store data faster than relational databases for every kind of bulk load.
options.why: Bulk loading is not the main benefit and graphs are not universally faster.

options.text: It lets testers skip defining migration objects because the graph infers the mapping itself.
options.why: Mapping rules still have to be defined and approved.

questions.explanation: Nodes are business entities and rules; edges are dependencies and lineage. Use it to choose test scope, sequence loads (customers before orders) and explain failures.

questions.prompt: Which practices make data migration tests reliable in a repeatable mock cycle? Select all that apply.

options.text: Automate source-to-target comparisons per migration object so every mock run is checked the same way.
options.why: Right: repeatability and speed matter when you rehearse many times.

options.text: Make loads re-runnable and idempotent, with reset scripts for the target.
options.why: Right: a failed mock must be rerunnable without manual cleanup.

options.text: Rely on a few manual spot checks in the SAP GUI after each load.
options.why: Spot checks miss systematic errors and do not scale to millions of rows.

options.text: Test only clean records and leave out historical data with known defects.
options.why: Dirty and edge-case data is exactly where migrations fail.

questions.explanation: Add a data-quality dashboard: rejected rows by reason, reconciliation status by object and trend by mock run.

questions.text: Data migration validation compares {1} counts, control {2} such as amounts and balances, and sampled field-level {3} between the legacy system and S/4HANA.
questions.explanation: Row counts catch loss, totals catch value drift, field-level checks catch mapping errors.

questions.prompt: Match each middle-mile logistics term to its meaning.

right.text: A shipper offers a load to a carrier, who may accept or reject it
A marketplace where carriers browse and book available loads
A carrier advertises where and when a truck is free so matching loads can be booked
An arrival or departure event raised when a GPS position crosses a facility boundary
One-off loads at current market rates versus committed capacity at agreed rates

questions.explanation: Middle-mile means freight moving between facilities such as fulfilment centres, sort centres and delivery stations, rather than to the final customer.

questions.prompt: US rules limit a property-carrying driver to 11 hours of driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty. A driver has already driven 8 hours. How many more driving hours remain, ignoring other limits?
questions.explanation: 11 - 8 = 3. A tracking and ETA system must account for such limits: an ETA that needs 6 more driving hours implies a mandatory rest stop, so the ETA is later than distance divided by speed.

questions.prompt: GPS and status events for trucks are published to a Kafka topic for ETA computation. Which design keeps each trip's events in order and the ETA correct?

options.text: Key messages by trip id, make consumers idempotent, and order by event time.
options.why: Right: one partition per key keeps order; dedupe and event time absorb retries and late data.

options.text: Use a random key so load spreads evenly, then sort globally at query time in the UI.
options.why: Random keys lose per-trip ordering in the stream and make stateful processing hard.

options.text: Use a single partition for the entire topic and a single consumer to guarantee strict ordering.
options.why: It would order everything but cannot scale to a large fleet.

options.text: Disable retries in the producer so that duplicates can never appear in the topic at all.
options.why: Without retries events can be lost; the correct fix is idempotent handling.

questions.explanation: Kafka orders messages only within a partition. Add a geofence service for arrival and departure events and recompute the ETA from the latest position, speed and driver hours.

questions.prompt: A property-carrying driver comes on duty at 06:00 after 10 hours off and, ignoring the sleeper-berth split rule, takes a 3-hour off-duty break during the day. At which hour of the day (24-hour clock) does the 14-hour window end?
questions.explanation: 06:00 + 14 hours = 20:00. Off-duty time inside the window does not extend it (FMCSA summary), so the break does not push the cutoff to 23:00. An ETA service must apply both the 11-hour driving limit and this 14-hour window, plus the 30-minute break rule.

questions.prompt: Customer master data sits in a non-SAP legacy billing system that exports CSV files. Which Migration Cockpit approach fits?

options.text: Fill migration templates or staging tables from the files, then simulate and load.
options.why: Right: staging tables or file templates are the route for non-SAP sources.

options.text: Direct transfer, because it reads the CSV files straight from the legacy file server.
options.why: Direct transfer reads from a connected SAP source system, not from arbitrary files.

options.text: Selective data transition, because it converts the legacy billing system in place.
options.why: That is a project approach for SAP systems, not a loading method for CSV data.

options.text: Real-time database replication, because the cockpit subscribes to the billing system's log.
options.why: The cockpit is a batch load tool and does not consume database logs.

questions.explanation: Rule of thumb: SAP-to-SAP data can use direct transfer (where released for your scope), anything else goes through files or staging tables. Always simulate before the real load.

questions.prompt: Tracking events arrive duplicated and out of order. Table trip_state(trip_id PRIMARY KEY, ts, lat, lon) keeps only the latest position per trip. Write a PostgreSQL upsert for one event ($1 trip_id, $2 ts, $3 lat, $4 lon) that never replaces a row with an older or equal ts.

checks.label: only when the new ts is newer

questions.model:
INSERT INTO trip_state (trip_id, ts, lat, lon)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)
ON CONFLICT (trip_id) DO UPDATE
  SET ts = EXCLUDED.ts, lat = EXCLUDED.lat, lon = EXCLUDED.lon
  WHERE EXCLUDED.ts > trip_state.ts;
questions.explanation: The WHERE on the DO UPDATE branch gives last-writer-wins by event time: a duplicate (equal ts) and a late arrival (older ts) both change nothing, so the consumer is idempotent and order-insensitive. Other shapes pass, for example a stored procedure that compares first. With at-least-once, unordered feeds, dedupe plus event-time ordering are the two core tricks.
